notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 16:43–63, drawn from the sources listed and organized by verse. Each point is followed by its URL.

---

## Ezekiel 16:43–63 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 43 — "Because you did not remember the days of your youth, but enraged Me with all these things, I will surely bring your deeds down upon your own head…"

- The root cause of judgment is "spiritual amnesia" — forgetting what God did for Israel in her youth. This repeats the charge from v. 22. The verb "fretted" (KJV) is better rendered "raged against me"; it is the same word used in 2 Kings 19:27–28 for rebellious raging. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The Hebrew perfect tense ("I will surely bring") presents the punishment as a completed fact, which then leads into the new section (vv. 44ff.) that provides further justification for God's judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-43.html — Keil & Delitzsch)
- The phrase "thou shalt not commit this lewdness" is difficult. Following the Masoretic pointing, many take it as second person. But Keil and Hengstenberg argue it should be read in the first person: "that I may not commit wickedness concerning all thine abominations" — i.e., God would be complicit in sin if He let it go unpunished, referencing Leviticus 19:29 where tolerating a daughter's whoredom is called *zimmah*. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-43.html)
- Gill notes that Israel "raged" against God — finding fault with Him for their calamities rather than repenting — and therefore God would recompense the fruit of her lewd ways upon her own head. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds that God would not let Israel fix blame for their suffering on Him; if He condoned their whoredoms without just punishment, He would be party to them (Leviticus 19:29). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 44 — "Behold, all who speak in proverbs will quote this proverb about you: 'Like mother, like daughter.'"

- A new section (the second parable in the chapter) begins here. The "mother" is the Canaanite race of Hittites and Amorites, whose immoral nature Israel adopted. The proverb means: the daughter (Jerusalem) shares the character of her mother (the Canaanite peoples). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html — Preacher's Complete Homiletical)
- Dyer notes this introduces the second parable: Jerusalem and her wicked sisters Samaria and Sodom. If her depraved sisters were judged, how could more-wicked Jerusalem escape? (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1635-50)
- Bible.org adds: this denotes that children take on the characteristics of the families in which they are raised (cf. Deut. 5:9). (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-16)

---

### v. 45 — "You are the daughter of your mother, who despised her husband and children. You are the sister of your sisters… Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite."

- "Your mother a Hittite and your father an Amorite" refers back to Ezekiel 16:3. These two tribes are put for all the Canaanite nations because they were the most prominent and wicked (cf. Gen. 15:16). It is a spiritual, not ethnic, genealogy — Israel's character was Canaanite. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The phrase "despised her husband and children" applied to Samaria and Sodom as well: though heathen, they are viewed as having gone astray from primeval revelation and proved false to the only true God, whom they once had known. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- Trapp says: the wife loathing husband and children depicts the unnaturalness of idolatry. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 46 — "Your older sister was Samaria, who lived with her daughters to your north; and your younger sister was Sodom, who lived with her daughters to your south."

- "Older" and "younger" (literally "greater" and "smaller" in Hebrew) refer to size/prominence, not chronology. Samaria was the capital of the larger northern kingdom; Sodom was a single city. Chronologically, Sodom was not younger than Jerusalem. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- Orientals described geography facing east: Samaria (north) was at the left, Sodom (south) at the right. Sodom is spoken of poetically as if still in existence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- "Her daughters" refers to the surrounding villages socially and economically connected to these walled cities (vv. 49, 55, 57, 61). (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-16)
- The three cities represent three capital cities that all experienced God's judgment: Samaria (taken by Assyria in 722 BC), Sodom (destroyed in Genesis 18–19), and Jerusalem (taken by Babylon in 586 BC). (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-16)

---

### v. 47 — "And you not only walked in their ways and practiced their abominations, but soon you were more depraved than they were."

- The Hebrew construction means: "You did not merely walk a little in their ways… but you acted more corruptly than they in all your ways." Jerusalem far outstripped both sisters in sin. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- This excess of wickedness is constantly charged against Judah (cf. Ezek. 5:6–7). Sodom sinned grievously in its day, but more than 1,000 years had passed, during which resistance to divine admonitions led to still deeper wickedness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary emphasizes that Jerusalem had greater light: the temple, sacrifices, divinely appointed priests, and the Law — advantages over others who practiced idolatry. Greater light means greater responsibility. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 48 — "As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, your sister Sodom and her daughters never did as you and your daughters have done."

- God swears by His own life ("As I live") to underscore the shocking verdict: Sodom — the proverbial epitome of wickedness — never sank to Jerusalem's depths. This is meant to stun the hearers. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)
- Jesus Himself later used a similar comparison: it would be more tolerable for Sodom in the day of judgment than for the cities that rejected Him (Matt. 10:15; 11:24). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 49 — "Now this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy."

- This is the classic biblical definition of Sodom's sin *beyond* the sexual deviance described in Genesis 19. Ezekiel identifies pride, excess of food (gluttony), undisturbed ease (complacency), and neglect of the poor and needy as Sodom's foundational iniquity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- Bible.org notes: Genesis 19 describes Sodom's sexual deviation, but here she is condemned for lack of care for the poor. YHWH cares for the poor, alien, outcast, orphan, and socially disenfranchised (cf. Deut. 10:18; 14:29; 24:17–22). (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-16)
- This verse is frequently cited in social-justice discussions across traditions: Sodom's root sin was not homosexuality alone but a whole complex of pride, affluence, idleness, and hard-heartedness toward the needy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

---

### v. 50 — "Thus they were haughty and committed abominations before Me. Therefore I removed them, as you have seen."

- Pride led to abominations. The sequence is: arrogance → complacency → neglect of the poor → haughtiness → abominable acts → judgment. God "removed" (literally "swept away") Sodom when He saw it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The word "abominations" (*toebah*) refers to loathsome, detestable things — particularly idolatrous and immoral practices. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)

---

### v. 51 — "Furthermore, Samaria did not commit half the sins you did. You have multiplied your abominations beyond theirs, and all the abominations you have committed have made your sisters appear righteous."

- Samaria (the northern kingdom) fell to Assyria about 130 years before Jerusalem's fall; Judah had far more time to indulge in sin and far more light (the temple, priesthood, Davidic kings). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)
- Jamieson says: Samaria was less guilty than Judah, for Judah betrayed greater ingratitude, having greater privileges — the temple, the priesthood, and the regular order of kings. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)
- "Made your sisters appear righteous" — Judah's sins were so egregious that Sodom and Samaria seemed almost innocent by comparison. This is a cutting indictment, especially since the name "Sodom" was not even spoken by Jews out of contempt for its evil. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)
- Jesus employed the same logic in Matthew 12:41–42 regarding Nineveh and the Queen of the South. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)

---

### v. 52 — "So now you must bear your disgrace, since you have brought justification for your sisters… your sins were more vile than theirs."

- Because Judah's sins were more abominable, Sodom and Samaria "appear more righteous" — not actually righteous, but relatively so by comparison. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)
- The phrase "you have made judgment favorable for your sisters" (NASB) or "brought justification for your sisters" means Judah's extreme guilt made her sisters' guilt look less severe. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-16)
- The repeated imperatives — "bear your disgrace," "be ashamed" — emphasize that this shame is a judicial sentence. Judah had judged her sisters (v. 56); now she must bear her own shame. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 53 — "But I will restore Sodom and her daughters from captivity, as well as Samaria and her daughters. And I will restore you along with them."

- The Hebrew idiom "restore the captivity" (*shub shebuth*) often means "restore the fortunes" rather than literal return from exile. This is confirmed by usage in Job 42:10 (Job never went into captivity) and by ancient Aramaic parallels. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)
- Charles Feinberg notes: "There are instances — e.g., Job 42:10; Ezek 16:53 (a prediction concerning Sodom) — where captivity is not in view. In such cases a derived meaning such as 'reverse or restore the fortunes' fits well." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)
- **A key interpretive question:** Does this promise a literal restoration of Sodom? Most traditional commentators take it as "restoration of fortunes" — not that the ancient city of Sodom will be rebuilt, but that the region/peoples represented by these cities will share in eschatological blessing. The Bridgeway Bible Commentary sees it as: after the overthrow of Babylon, the three regions of Palestine represented by these three cities would be restored and inhabited again. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The order is significant: Sodom and Samaria are restored *before* Jerusalem, "in order that she may bear her disgrace and be ashamed" (v. 54). Jerusalem, the most privileged, is last to be restored. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- Ellicott sees this passage as first declaring restoration "impossible" (vv. 53–59) in the strongest terms, then making an exception for a remnant in vv. 60–63. He argues that efforts to transform vv. 53–59 into a covert promise of restoration "are entirely unsuccessful." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 54 — "So you will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all you did to comfort them."

- The restoration is designed to produce shame and humiliation in Jerusalem, not pride. She "comforted" her sisters — perhaps by her own fall, which made Sodom and Samaria feel less alone in their judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The word "comfort" here may be ironic: Jerusalem's downfall brought a kind of consolation to her sisters because they were no longer the only ones disgraced. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

---

### v. 55 — "And your sisters, Sodom with her daughters and Samaria with her daughters, will return to their former state. You and your daughters will also return to your former state."

- "Return to their former state" echoes the "restore the fortunes" idiom. It means a *restitutio in integrum* — a restoration to the situation that prevailed earlier. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)
- This promise awaits full realization in the messianic kingdom. As Jamieson says: "the full realization of the restoration is yet future." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)

---

### v. 56 — "Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride…"

- In her days of pride, Jerusalem would not even speak Sodom's name — it was a byword too shameful to mention. Yet now Jerusalem's own reputation had become just as bad (v. 57). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: Jerusalem "did not open her mouth to acknowledge that her sins were comparable to those of Sodom, though they were." Boasting in the temple and their chosen lineage, they disregarded any need for repentance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 57 — "…before your wickedness was uncovered? Even so, you are now scorned by the daughters of Edom… and by the daughters of the Philistines…"

- The nations that once heard Jerusalem scorn Sodom now scorn Jerusalem herself. Edom and Philistia — hereditary enemies — are specifically named. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The BSB reads "daughters of Edom" (following some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions; other manuscripts read "daughters of Aram/Syria"). Either way, the point is that surrounding pagan nations now despise Jerusalem. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)

---

### v. 58 — "You will bear the consequences of your lewdness and your abominations, declares the LORD."

- A summary statement: Jerusalem has "paid for" (or "borne the penalty of") her lewdness. The judgment is presented as a completed fact. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The brevity underscores the finality: God's word closes the case. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

---

### v. 59 — "For this is what the Lord GOD says: I will deal with you according to your deeds, since you have despised the oath by breaking the covenant."

- The principle is strict retributive justice: "I will deal with you as you have done." The specific charge is despising the oath and breaking the covenant — the marriage-like covenant made at Sinai (Exodus 24:7–8). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-16.html)
- Matthew Henry notes that this verse concludes the warning of judgments: "After a full warning of judgments, mercy is remembered, mercy is reserved." The covenant-breaking is what makes the coming grace in v. 60 so stunning. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 60 — "But I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you."

- **The great turning point.** "Nevertheless" marks a dramatic shift: despite covenant-breaking by Israel, God will remember *His* covenant and establish an everlasting one. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)
- **Keil (Reformed/Lutheran):** The covenant God made in Israel's "youth" (the Exodus/Sinai covenant) will be established as an *everlasting* covenant. It is not an entirely new covenant but the perfecting of the old one for everlasting duration. This is linked to the "sure mercies of David" (Isa. 55:3; 2 Sam. 23:5) — the covenant rests not on law-keeping but on the forgiving grace of God (cf. v. 63 with Jer. 31:31–34). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Trapp (Puritan/Anglican):** "Here beginneth the evangelical part of the chapter, which is for the comfort of the elect, who would be frightened to hear those direful threats." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** The "everlasting covenant" traces back to the *Abrahamic* covenant (Gen. 17:7, 19), not the Sinai covenant. It is "purely of blessing, and in the form of it entirely unconditional" (Gal. 3:17). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik/Pentecostal):** Despite the certainty of judgment, God would not forget His covenant. The coming judgment would be so great that Israel would be tempted to believe there was no more hope — yet again and again Yahweh promised to establish His covenant. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)
- **Gill (Baptist):** God will remember the covenant made with Israel in her youth as she left Egypt and will establish an everlasting covenant — "a new covenant, only in the sense that He will extend and perfect the old one," linked to the sure mercies of David and the promise to Abraham. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)
- Bible.org identifies this as the "new covenant" of Jer. 31:31–34, also described in Ezek. 36:22–38. The three promises are: (a) "I will remember My covenant" (cf. Lev. 26:42, 45); (b) "I will establish an everlasting covenant"; (c) "when I have forgiven you for all that you have done" (v. 63). (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-16)

---

### v. 61 — "Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed when you receive your older and younger sisters. I will give them to you as daughters, but not because of My covenant with you."

- The restoration brings humility: Israel will "remember" her ways and "be ashamed" — not a destructive shame but a penitent, saving shame (like Ezra's and the publican's). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **"I will give them to you as daughters"** — Jerusalem will receive Sodom and Samaria as "daughters," i.e., they will come under her authority and care. This inverts the earlier sister relationship and points to Jerusalem's future preeminence in God's kingdom. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)
- **"But not because of My covenant with you"** (or "not by thy covenant" — KJV): The Sinai covenant excluded other nations (Exod. 24:7); the blessings to all nations flow from the earlier promise to Abraham (Gen. 12:1–3). As the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary explains: the blessings to all nations come "not by national covenant at Sinai but solely by His grace… from God's promise to Abraham" (Gal. 3:13–14; 4:26). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Trapp:** "Not by thy covenant — Made with thee in Mount Sinai, but by a covenant of grace made in Mount Zion." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: the blessings to all nations flow from God's promise to Abraham (Gen. 12:1–3), not His covenant with Israel at Sinai or Horeb. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 62 — "So I will establish My covenant with you, and you will know that I am the LORD."

- The phrase is repeated for emphasis (from v. 60). The establishment of the covenant results in the knowledge of God — "you will know that I am the LORD," the signature recognition formula of Ezekiel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)
- **Ellicott:** The old covenant, having failed, is merged in the new and better covenant promised in Ezek. 11:19; 18:31, and more fully in Jer. 31:31–34. This new covenant, established through a perfect Mediator, alone can perfectly fulfil God's gracious designs. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Trapp:** "My new spiritual and eternal covenant, grounded upon the Messias, and made with the whole Israel according to faith. Jeremiah 31:31–34; 2 Corinthians 3:3; Hebrews 8:8." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html)
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary sees this as the covenant pledged at Sinai but now transformed: "His blessing other nations, in that Golden millennial era, will not weaken or impoverish Israel in her restored glory" (Gal. 3:17). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 63 — "…so that when I make atonement for all you have done, you will remember and be ashamed and never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, declares the Lord GOD."

- **"When I make atonement"** — the Hebrew word (*kaphar*) is the technical term used in the Law for the atonement or "covering up" of sins. The Pulpit Commentary renders it "when I pardon thee," emphasizing that God Himself provides the atonement. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/16-63.htm)
- **"Never open your mouth anymore"** — this is the silence of the truly penitent: no self-justification, no murmuring against God, no excusing of sin. As JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown) says: "never open thy mouth — in vindication, or even palliation, of thyself, or expostulation with God for His dealings (Rom. 3:19), when thou seest thine own exceeding unworthiness, and My superabounding grace." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/16-63.htm)
- **Gill:** The more believers know of God in Christ and of Him as their covenant God, the more they remember former evil ways with shame and confusion. God is "pacified" (propitiated) not by human obedience, repentance, or faith, but by the blood and sacrifice of Christ. This produces silence — no more excusing sin or commending one's own righteousness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/16-63.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "The Divine mercy should be powerful to melt our hearts into godly sorrow for sin. Nor will God ever leave the sinner to perish, who is humbled for his sins, and comes to trust in His mercy and grace through Jesus Christ." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Trapp:** "Never open thy mouth — To extenuate thy sins, or to murmur at thy sufferings; but be silent and submissive." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary:** The chapter ends at the threshold of the new dispensation: "Jerusalem humbled and bearing her shame, yet in the abjectness of her self-accusation realising the end towards which the love of Jehovah had guided her from the beginning." The permanence of the new relation is expressed by the "everlasting covenant, which cannot be broken because based on the forgiveness of sin and a renewal of heart." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-16.html)
- Enduring Word: "Through Ezekiel, the LORD hinted at the nature of the future covenant. The idea of a God-provided atonement is an important aspect of the new covenant, already mentioned in Ezekiel 11:17–21. This would be the true and ultimate restoration of Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

---

## Tradition-Specific Differences

### On the Nature of the "Everlasting Covenant" (vv. 60, 62)

The traditions largely agree that this points to the new covenant in Christ, but they frame it differently:

- **Reformed/Keil:** The everlasting covenant is the *perfection* of the old (Sinai) covenant, not something entirely new. It rests on forgiving grace, not law-keeping, and is linked to the Davidic promise (2 Sam. 7; Isa. 55:3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes):** Also sees continuity with the Abrahamic and Davidic covenants. Gill emphasizes the covenant of grace made with the elect; Garner-Howes sees a millennial fulfillment for national Israel alongside Gentile blessing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Emphasizes the personal, experiential dimension — God's faithfulness despite human unfaithfulness — and the hint at God-provided atonement that points to the new covenant. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)
- **Methodist/Holiness (Matthew Henry):** Emphasizes the transformative power of divine mercy to produce godly sorrow and repentance. The promise is "in part fulfilled at the return of the penitent and reformed Jews out of Babylon, but to have fuller accomplishment in gospel times." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** The old covenant must be *merged* into the new; it had "failed" and needed a perfect Mediator. The passage moves from declared impossibility of restoration (vv. 53–59) to the exception of grace (vv. 60–63). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

### On the Restoration of Sodom (v. 53)

- **Literal restoration view (some Baptists/dispensationalists):** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary seems to lean toward a literal future restoration: "God will restore departed glory to Jerusalem and Israel… Sodom and Samaria and their daughters will be restored, before Jerusalem." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Figurative/"restore fortunes" view (majority):** Most commentators, including Keil, Feinberg, and the NET Bible notes, see the idiom as "restore the fortunes" — a *restitutio in integrum* — applicable to Sodom not as a literal city but as representing peoples/regions that will share in eschatological blessing. Job 42:10 uses the same idiom for someone never in captivity. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)

### On the Identity of the Covenant in v. 61 ("not because of My covenant with you")

- **Sinai covenant view (majority):** "Not by thy covenant" means the Sinai covenant, which excluded Gentiles. Gentile inclusion comes through the Abrahamic covenant of grace. This is the view of Trapp, the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary, and Ellicott. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-16.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-16.html)
- **Gill:** Sees it as "not by national covenant at Sinai but solely by His grace." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

### On the Nature of Sodom's Sin (v. 49)

- Across traditions, Ezekiel 16:49 is universally cited to show Sodom's sin was not *only* sexual. However, there is nuance:
  - **Traditional/conservative:** The verse supplements Genesis 19, showing the root sins (pride, complacency, neglect of the poor) that *led to* the sexual abominations. Both are real.
  - **Some modern readers** use this verse to argue that Sodom's sin was *primarily* social injustice, not homosexuality. The traditional commentators do not draw this conclusion; they see v. 49 as describing the moral preconditions that produced the abominations of v. 50. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-16; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)

### Lutheran Perspective

- No dedicated Lutheran verse-by-verse source was found in the search results for this specific passage. The Keil & Delitzsch commentary (Lutheran/Reformed) was the closest, treating the passage within a covenantal framework that emphasizes God's unilateral grace. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/16-43.html)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes)

- The NET Bible notes (accessed via Precept Austin) provide linguistic precision, particularly regarding the idiom "restore the fortunes" (*shub shebuth*), which is documented in Old Aramaic texts (Sefire inscriptions) as meaning "to turn someone's fortune, bring about change" or "reestablish as it was." This does not always imply literal return from exile. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)
- The BSB text itself follows the NET in several places, including the rendering "restore … from captivity" where the Hebrew idiom is debated. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1651-63)
